document.title: Afghanistan: British Journalist Visits Site of Training Camps; HUA Activity Alleged (Islama 009994)
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), Pakistan: "The Taliban's Godfather"?
document.note: [Confidential] A British journalist who visited two training camps in Paktia on November 14, 1996 reports both appear occupied. Taliban sources say one is occupied by Harakat-ul-Ansar and the other by assorted foreigners including Chechens, Bosnian Muslims, Sudanese and other Arabs.

mentions.quote: REFUSED A MEETING WITH MULLAH SAYED ABDULLAH, THE TALIBAN GOVERNOR
A MESSAGE FROM HIM "DENYING THAT THE CAMPS ARE BEING USED AND WARNING HER NOT TO GO NEAR THEM."

events.description: Taliban seized/shut down the Al Badr camps formerly controlled by Hezb-i-Islami (Aug/Sep 1996).
British journalist visited the site of the Al Badr camps, saw them as 'occupied and active', but could not enter.
Journalist briefed a Political Officer and USIS Information Officer at the US Embassy about her visit.
US Embassy Islamabad cable 009994 reports the journalist's account.
British journalist Lees visited the site of the Al Badr training camps in Paktia Province but could not enter; camps looked occupied and active.
Lees briefed the Political Officer and USIS Information Officer on her visit to the camps.
Taliban seized/shut down the Al Badr camps formerly controlled by Hezb-i-Islami.
US Embassy Islamabad cabled State on the journalist's report and alleged HUA activity at the camps.

key_claims: A British journalist saw the Al Badr camps near Khost as occupied and active on 14 Nov 1996.
A Taliban source said one camp is occupied by HUA militants.
The other camp reportedly holds foreigners including Chechens, Bosnian Muslims, Sudanese and other Arabs.
Instructors are reportedly the same ones who taught there before the Taliban seizure in Aug/Sep 1996.
The Taliban governor of Khost denied camp use and warned the journalist away.
The embassy judges that the Al Badr camps are 'back in business' contrary to Taliban claims.
